Abstention means the deliberate, conscious choice to hold yourself back from doing something — especially something you are fully able to do, entitled to do, or even expected to do.

The single most important thing to understand about abstention is that it is active, not passive. It is not the same as forgetting, being absent, or being prevented from something. When someone abstains, they are present, capable, and aware — but they make a clear, intentional decision to step back and not participate.

A simple way to picture it: if someone offers you a piece of cake and you simply weren't in the room, you didn't abstain — you were just absent. But if the cake is right in front of you, you could eat it, yet you deliberately say "no, I'm choosing not to" — that is abstention. You had the full opportunity; you made a conscious choice to pass it up.

This is by far the most common and important context for this word. In any formal vote — in a parliament, a committee, a board meeting, or an international body like the United Nations — each eligible voter generally has three options: vote yes (in favor), vote no (against), or abstain.

An abstention here means a voter is present and fully entitled to vote, but chooses not to cast a vote for either side. It is a formal, recognized third option — and critically, it is not the same as simply being absent or not showing up to the vote. The person showed up; they just chose not to pick a side.

People abstain in a vote for a variety of reasons. They might feel they don't have enough information to make a fair and informed judgment. They might have a personal conflict of interest — meaning they have something to personally gain or lose from the outcome — and feel it would be inappropriate for them to take a side. They might disagree with how a question is being framed and feel that voting yes or no would misrepresent their actual position. Or they might be sending a deliberate political signal — expressing dissatisfaction or neutrality without going as far as outright opposing something.

It's also worth knowing that an abstention is never truly "neutral" in its real-world effect. In many formal bodies, the rules determine whether abstentions count toward the total votes needed to pass a decision. So depending on the system, an abstention can influence the outcome just as surely as a yes or no vote — just in a more indirect way. This is exactly why abstentions in major votes — such as those in the United Nations Security Council — are closely watched and considered politically meaningful.

Outside of voting, abstention describes the deliberate choice to hold back from a specific activity, usually one that is tempting, pleasurable, or habitual.

If a person who enjoys alcohol goes to a party and consciously chooses not to drink, they are practicing abstention from alcohol. If someone on a diet resists dessert despite wanting it, that is an abstention from sugar. If a person stays silent during a heated argument even though they have plenty they could say, that is an abstention from speech.

The common thread in all these cases is self-restraint combined with willpower. The person could do the thing — nothing is stopping them from the outside. But they choose, entirely of their own will, not to do it.

These two words are closely related and often confused, so understanding the difference is worthwhile.

Abstinence refers to an ongoing, usually long-term or even permanent commitment to avoiding something. It often relates to physical pleasures or deeply ingrained habits — like abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, or sexual activity. It implies a sustained, lifestyle-level choice rather than a one-off decision.

Abstention tends to refer to a single act or specific instance of refraining — especially in a formal, situational context like a vote or a particular moment of temptation.

A rough way to remember the distinction: abstinence is a way of living, while abstention is more often a single act or decision in a given moment. That said, in casual everyday speech, the two words are sometimes used interchangeably, and the distinction isn't always rigidly maintained outside of formal writing or legal contexts.

Knowing the related forms of the word helps you recognize and use it naturally in different sentences.

Abstain is the verb — the action word. ("She chose to abstain from the vote." / "He abstained from eating processed food all month.")

Abstaining is the present participle, used for ongoing action. ("Three members are abstaining from the decision.")

Abstained is the past tense. ("The delegate abstained during the final round of voting.")

Abstentions is the plural noun form. ("There were five abstentions recorded in the final count.")

Abstention is the deliberate, intentional act of not doing something you could do — most powerfully used when talking about voting (choosing neither yes nor no as a formal position) and in personal behavior (consciously choosing to hold back from an activity or temptation). Its defining quality is always intentionality: abstention is never an accident or an oversight. It is a choice made by someone who is fully capable of participating but decides, for their own reasons, not to.
